fetched_contents.text: CO2, NOx and SOx removal from flue gas via microalgae cultivation: A critical review - Yen - 2015 - Biotechnology Journal Review , Hong-Wei Yen Department of Chemical and Materials Engineering, Taichung, Taiwan Search for more papers by this author Shih-Hsin Ho, Shih-Hsin Ho Organization of Advanced Science and Technology, Kobe University, Kobe, Japan Search for more papers by this author Chun-Yen Chen, Chun-Yen Chen Center for Bioscience and Biotechnology, National Cheng Kung University, Tainan, Taiwan Search for more papers by this author Jo-Shu Chang, Corresponding Author Jo-Shu Chang * changjs@mail.ncku.edu.tw Center for Bioscience and Biotechnology, National Cheng Kung University, Tainan, Taiwan Research Center for Energy Technology and Strategy, National Cheng Kung University, Tainan, Taiwan Department of Chemical Engineering, National Cheng Kung University, Tainan, Taiwan Correspondence: Prof. Jo-Shu Chang, Department of Chemical Engineering, National Cheng Kung University, Tainan 701, TaiwanSearch for more papers by this author First published: 30 April 2015 Abstract Flue gas refers to the gas emitting from the combustion processes, and it contains CO2, NOx, SOx and other potentially hazardous compounds. Due to the increasing concerns of CO2 emissions and environmental pollution, the cleaning process of flue gas has attracted much attention. Using microalgae to clean up flue gas via photosynthesis is considered a promising CO2 mitigation process for flue gas. However, the impurities in the flue gas may inhibit microalgal growth, leading to a lower microalgae-based CO2 fixation rate. The inhibition effects of SOx that contribute to the low pH could be alleviated by maintaining a stable pH level, while NOx can be utilized as a nitrogen source to promote microalgae growth when it dissolves and is oxidized in the culture medium. The yielded microalgal biomass from fixing flue gas CO2 and utilizing NOx and SOx as nutrients would become suitable feedstock to produce biofuels and bio-based chemicals. In addition to the removal of SOx, NOx and CO2, using microalgae to remove heavy metals from flue gas is also quite attractive. In conclusion, the use of microalgae for simultaneous removal of CO2, SOx and NOx from flue gas is an environmentally benign process and represents an ideal platform for CO2 reutilization. Introduction Climate change and environmental safety action with growing water pollutants globally remain the most complex challenges that present and future generations of humankind face and raise several security risks. The evidence of security risks arising from these challenges in the Global South provides forward-looking perspectives on increasing the resilience of affected individuals and communities. It is crucial to demonstrate different strategies as key elements to drive a transformation toward greater sustainability and resilience (Thorn et al., 2023). The demand for energy from fossil fuels is continuously increasing with the growth in the world population in recent years, which has led to increased emissions of greenhouse gases (GHGs). However, using fossil fuels is an environmentally unsustainable source because the GHGs cause global warming (Sial et al., 2021). Since the late nineteenth century, increased carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions have reached their highest level in the last thirty-five years, particularly after 2010, due to anthropogenic activities that have raised the earth’s average surface temperature by 1.1 °C (Gür, 2022). One-third of total CO2 emissions are from fossil fuel combustion in power plants. The highest value of CO2 concentration, from 280 ppm to 420 ppm, in the last decade has led to global climate change and biological extinction. Currently, over 33.1 GT of CO2 is emitted into the atmosphere, including a significant portion of carbon (C) associated with direct combustion (Qin et al., 2021). The complex challenges associated with CO2 generation and emissions (increased by 1.7% annually) make them difficult to address and undermine the adaptive capacities of affected individuals and societies. Climate change erodes agricultural production and disrupts food supplies (Nguyen et al., 2023). The Paris Agreement was ratified in 2016 to mitigate, adapt, and finance strategies to tackle GHG emissions. The agreement's goal was to limit global warming to 1.5 °C. Given the current situation, the World Meteorological Organization envisages that the global average temperature will be raised to 3–5 °C by 2100 (Gebel et al., 2022). Therefore, the strategies to deal with CO2 emissions involve: * • Reduction of non-renewable energy sources such as the use of fossil fuels. * • Optimize and enhance low-C emission renewable energy sources, including carbon-neutral technologies. * • Utilization of carbon capture and storage as post-treatment technologies. Recent research has described carbon dioxide capture storage (CCS) and sequestration technologies. Therefore, there is a need to achieve environmental and economic sustainability. For example, future fuel production processes must be renewable and capable of sequestering atmospheric carbon dioxide. So, shifting from fossil fuels to low-carbon fuels becomes the highest priority. The most effective ways to reduce CO2 emissions are to improve the energy efficiency of each economic sector and to reduce the cutting of tropical and temperate forests around the world (Tang et al., 2022). These methods, however, may not be able to control CO2 emissions due to various political and socio-economic barriers, so other more innovative and less well-defined CO2 mitigation measures are required. The most practical of these innovations is to increase CO2 sinks through photosynthesis, including increased carbon storage in standing tree biomass, the substitution of fossil fuels with biofuels, an increase in soil carbon sequestration, and an increase in soil primary productivity (Zahoor et al., 2022). Microalgae can be extensively used to capture CO2 from power plants, steel, cement, oil, automobiles, and many other industries. The resulting algal biomass can be used not only for biofuel production but also for various industrial products. Besides giving environmental and economic benefits, large scale algae cultivation can create millions of jobs at different levels of society (Tarafdar et al., 2023). Much work has been done on carbon sequestration and algae biofuel production, but it still needs much research to meet the increasing energy demand. We hope that biofuel will replace fossil fuels to a larger extent and reduce atmospheric CO2 to combat Global warming (Nguyen et al., 2023). Renewable energy sources are considered an alternative to fossil fuels due to low C footprints (Yadav and Mondal, 2022). Biological CCS technologies have gained popularity due to their ability to convert C sources into valuable products (Daneshvar et al., 2022; Shahbaz et al., 2021). Bioethanol and biodiesel are currently available renewable energy sources from conventional crops. However, crop production and price pose a real challenge for these sources. Therefore, biofuel production from microalgae could be a potential source that does not interfere with human food (Onyeaka et al., 2021). Microalgal cultivation has advantages over crop-based production, such as high biomass production, less land cultivation requirement, and low cost per yield. CO2, water, nutrients, and sunlight are required to grow microalgae, but water and inorganic nutrients are limiting factors in using microalgae as a biofuel source. fetched_contents.text: Physiological and enzymatic responses of Chlorella vulgaris exposed to produced water and its potential for bioremediation Environ Monit Assess. 2019 May 27;191(6):399. doi: 10.1007/s10661-019-7519-8. Authors Affiliations * 1 Research Group in Aquatic and Environmental Biotechnology and Toxicology - BioTox, Animal Sciences School, Faculty of Agricultural Sciences and Natural Resources, Universidad de los Llanos, km 12 vía Puerto López, vereda Barcelona, Villavicencio, Meta, Colombia. * 2 Research Group in Aquatic and Environmental Biotechnology and Toxicology - BioTox, Animal Sciences School, Faculty of Agricultural Sciences and Natural Resources, Universidad de los Llanos, km 12 vía Puerto López, vereda Barcelona, Villavicencio, Meta, Colombia. ymvelascos@unillanos.edu.co. * PMID: 31134347 * DOI: 10.1007/s10661-019-7519-8 Abstract In South America, Colombia is known as an important oil-producing country. However, the environmental impact of crude oil industry has not been studied deeply and few studies have been carried out for evaluating responses of algae and its adaptation under specific conditions. Enzymatic and physiological effects in Chlorella vulgaris and its potential for bioremediation after exposure to produced water (PW) were assessed using different PW concentrations (0, 25, 50, 75 and 100%) and crude oil. Variables such as cell density, growth rate (μ), percentage of growth inhibition (% I), chlorophyll a and b and cell diameter were evaluated during 5 days. Furthermore, enzymatic biomarkers such as superoxide dismutase (SOD) and catalase (CAT) were also measured. Results showed that the treatment with 100% PW had the highest cell density and μ; similarly, 25% PW treatment had a similar behaviour, being these two treatments with the highest growth. A dose-dependent response was seen for chlorophyll a and b and cell diameter, showing significant differences between treatments and the control. Different levels of SOD and CAT were observed in algae exposed to PW. At 24 h, an increase in SOD and CAT activity was observed, probably due to effects caused by xenobiotics. After 72 h, a decrease in the activity of both enzymes was observed. The results evidenced that C. vulgaris can adapt easily to PW, showing an increase on its growth and stabilisation in its antioxidant activity. Strain performance comparison across growth, biomass, and gas utilization

The evidence available for strain performance under gas conditions similar to coke oven exhaust is mixed but sufficient to identify broad trends rather than a complete strain-by-strain ranking. The clearest direct result is that some microalgae strains, including one Chlorella sp. strain designated MTF-15, showed higher growth rates in flue gas from varied sources of coke oven, hot stove, and similar combustion processes [N1-R1]. This suggests that strain-specific growth response is meaningful under such conditions, though the evidence does not give a full list of competing strains or a standardized comparison across many isolates.

For biomass yield, the evidence points to higher growth in some conditions rather than a single universal “best” strain. In one study, the 100% produced water (PW) treatment gave the highest cell density and growth rate for Chlorella vulgaris, while the 25% PW treatment also showed strong growth behavior [N3-F3]. This is relevant because it shows that strain adaptation and environmental stress can strongly influence biomass outcomes, even though the condition here is PW rather than coke oven exhaust. It also implies that biomass yield is not fixed by strain alone: growth can be shaped by both intrinsic strain traits and extrinsic environmental stressors.

CO2 utilization and gas utilization rates are more clearly supported in the evidence. Chlorella vulgaris can tolerate and effectively utilize elevated CO2 concentrations, with reported effectiveness under fed-batch culture [N1-R4]. A review also states that microalgae can assimilate CO2 from flue gas via photosynthesis and that NOx can be used as a nitrogen source when dissolved and oxidized, which may help growth [N1-F1]. This is important because it indicates that CO2 utilization is often biological assimilation, rather than merely a physical absorption effect. The evidence also notes that the impurities in flue gas may inhibit microalgal growth, so gas toxicity is a real constraint [N1-F1].

For other gases, the evidence is less specific on exact utilization rates for NOx and SO2. A review states that SOx may contribute to low pH and that pH stability can alleviate inhibition effects [N1-F1]. It also states that NOx can be utilized as a nitrogen source when dissolved and oxidized [N1-F1]. These statements suggest that gas utilization is not uniform: NOx appears to be assimilated or at least partially usable, whereas SOx may primarily affect pH and inhibit growth rather than being directly assimilated. The evidence does not clearly separate strain-specific utilization rates for these gases, so any comparison across strains is weakly supported by the provided material.

Growth limitation factors are better documented. The evidence explicitly states that impurities in flue gas may inhibit microalgal growth [N1-F1]. It also notes that SOx can contribute to low pH and that pH stability helps alleviate inhibition [N1-F1]. Additionally, the evidence on produced water shows that strain adaptation is possible but that growth is still influenced by stress and nutrient conditions [N3-F3]. Taken together, this suggests that growth under coke oven exhaust conditions is limited by gas toxicity and pH, with nutrient availability also playing a role when the culture is stressed.

Simulation conditions and gas composition strongly affect reported performance. The review notes that the effect of SOx and NOx on CO2 fixation depends on algae cell density, SOx and NOx concentration, gas flow rate, and reactor design [N6-R5]. Another study on simulated flue gas exposure found that microalgal protein content decreased under simulated power plant emissions, showing that simulated conditions can alter physiological outcomes [N6-R2]. The evidence also emphasizes that CO2 removal and other gas-phase effects depend on reactor parameters and gas composition [N6-R4]. These findings indicate that reported strain performance is highly context-dependent: a strain that performs well in one gas composition or reactor setup may not do so under another.

Overall, the evidence supports a cautious conclusion: some strains of Chlorella vulgaris, particularly those adapted to high CO2 or flue-gas-like conditions, can outperform others in biomass yield and CO2 utilization under coke oven exhaust conditions [N1-R1][N1-R4][N1-F1]. However, the evidence does not provide a strong enough comparative ranking of strains to identify a single “best” strain, and performance is heavily influenced by gas toxicity, pH, nutrient availability, and simulation conditions [N1-F1][N6-R5]. The available data also suggest that strain differences mainly affect CO2 and other gas utilization rates through physiological and metabolic adaptation, not through a uniform superior assimilation capacity [N3-F3][N3-R3].

Pollutant removal capacity and mechanism for coke oven exhaust gases

The evidence indicates that Chlorella vulgaris can remove multiple pollutants from flue gas, but the reported capacities and mechanisms differ by pollutant. For SO2, the evidence is consistent with removal through a combination of chemical and biological pathways. A review states that microalgae can remove SOx from flue gas via photosynthesis and that the effect of SOx and NOx on CO2 fixation depends on reactor conditions and gas composition [N6-R5]. Another review notes that the impurities in flue gas may inhibit microalgal growth, implying that removal is not simply physical adsorption but is constrained by toxicity and environmental stress [N1-F1]. The evidence also suggests that SOx can lower pH and that pH stability helps alleviate inhibition, which points to a chemical reaction pathway in addition to biological assimilation [N1-F1]. Overall, the evidence supports a mixed mechanism for SO2 removal: chemical interaction with the culture medium and possible biological assimilation, with removal efficiency depending on gas composition and reactor design [N1-F1][N6-R5].

For NOx, the evidence is more directly supportive of biological assimilation. A review explicitly states that NOx can be utilized as a nitrogen source when dissolved and oxidized in the culture medium [N1-F1]. A separate study on microalgal-bacterial systems reports a maximum CO2 removal efficiency of 55.3% at 0.15% CO2 in a membrane photobioreactor and mentions Chlorella vulgaris as part of the system [N2-R2]. While this does not directly measure NOx removal, it supports the idea that NOx can be assimilated into the culture when available in oxidized form. The evidence also indicates that NOx removal is part of a broader pollutant-removal process that may involve assimilation rather than purely physical adsorption [N1-F1].

For CO, the evidence is more indirect. The review notes that microalgae can remove CO2 from flue gas via photosynthesis, and the flue-gas-related evidence emphasizes CO2 mitigation and removal [N1-F1][N6-R5]. However, the provided material does not specifically report CO removal by Chlorella vulgaris under coke oven exhaust conditions. The closest related statement is that microalgae removal of CO2 depends on reactor conditions and gas composition [N6-R5]. Therefore, while the evidence supports CO2 removal as a major target pollutant, it does not provide a strong direct measure of CO removal for Chlorella vulgaris under coke-oven exhaust conditions.

For particulates, the evidence is very limited. The review mentions heavy-metal removal from flue gas as an attractive extension of microalgae use, but it does not specifically discuss particulate capture by Chlorella vulgaris [N1-F1]. The provided material therefore does not support a confident conclusion about particulate removal capacity.

The likely removal pathways are therefore: SO2 is removed by chemical interaction and possible assimilation, NOx by biological assimilation as nitrogen, CO2 by biological assimilation via photosynthesis, and particulates are not well supported by the evidence provided. The evidence also makes clear that removal is not dominated by physical adsorption in the way that some gas-phase processes might be; instead, it is constrained by toxicity, pH, and nutrient availability [N1-F1][N6-R5]. The removal efficiency of each pollutant depends strongly on gas composition and simulation conditions, including SOx and NOx concentration, cell density, gas flow rate, and reactor design [N6-R5].

Physiological and metabolic responses are relevant to explaining these differences. The evidence on Chlorella vulgaris exposed to produced water shows that growth can increase and antioxidant activity stabilize under stress, indicating that physiological adaptation is important for survival and pollutant removal [N3-F3]. A separate study on Chlorella strains exposed to high CO2 found different metabolic acclimation strategies and intracellular pH regulation, showing that strain-specific physiology can shape tolerance and utilization under gas stress [N3-R1][N3-R3]. These findings support the idea that pollutant removal capacity varies by strain because some strains may better regulate pH, stress responses, and nutrient assimilation than others [N3-F3][N3-R1].

In summary, the evidence suggests that Chlorella vulgaris can effectively remove SO2 and NOx from coke oven exhaust gases, with NOx more clearly assimilated as a nitrogen source and SO2 removed partly through chemical and partly through biological mechanisms [N1-F1][N6-R5]. CO2 removal is also strong, but the evidence does not provide a direct measure of CO removal under coke-oven conditions [N1-F1][N6-R5]. Pollutant removal is likely dominated by biological assimilation for NOx and CO2, with chemical interaction and pH regulation playing important roles for SO2 [N1-F1][N6-R5]. Gas composition and simulation conditions strongly affect removal efficiency, making strain performance highly context-dependent [N6-R5].

System-level constraints and optimization opportunities for industrial application

The evidence indicates that cultivating Chlorella vulgaris on coke oven exhaust gases is feasible, but several operational constraints must be managed for stable cultivation. First, gas flow rate is an important constraint because the review states that the effect of SOx and NOx on CO2 fixation depends on SOx and NOx concentration, gas flow rate, and reactor design [N6-R5]. The operational search evidence also suggests that reactor design and gas-phase effects are central to performance, with simulation conditions and gas composition strongly affecting reported strain performance [N5-R4][N6-R4]. This implies that gas flow rate cannot be arbitrarily increased without risking toxicity, mass transfer limitations, or reduced biomass productivity.

Second, temperature is an operational limit because the evidence on industrial exhaust gas cultivation notes that temperature affects microalgal growth and bioreactor performance [N5-R1][N5-R2]. The operational search evidence further shows that temperature and other operational parameters can significantly influence biomass productivity, with the example of C. vulgaris showing high biomass productivities up to 30°C with moderate to high CO2 [N5-R2]. This indicates that temperature is not universally optimal across all conditions; rather, it must be kept within a range that balances growth and pollutant capture while avoiding thermal stress or denaturation of enzymes and other physiological processes.

Third, pH is a major constraint because the review explicitly states that impurities in flue gas may inhibit microalgal growth and that SOx can contribute to low pH, which can be alleviated by maintaining a stable pH level [N1-F1]. The evidence on produced water also shows that growth can increase and antioxidant activity stabilize under stress, but the outcome still depends on environmental conditions [N3-F3]. Taken together, these findings suggest that pH control is essential: unstable or low pH can limit biomass production and pollutant removal, while stable pH supports better tolerance and assimilation of nutrients and pollutants [N1-F1][N3-F3].

Operational limits for stable cultivation therefore include: gas flow rate must be carefully controlled to avoid toxicity and mass transfer bottlenecks [N6-R5]; temperature should remain within a range that supports growth without thermal stress [N5-R2]; and pH should be stabilized to prevent inhibition from SOx and other impurities [N1-F1]. The evidence also suggests that nutrient availability is an underlying constraint, because growth under stress is shaped by both intrinsic strain adaptation and extrinsic nutrient conditions [N3-F3].

Opportunities to improve pollutant capture are substantial and are supported by both strain and system evidence. First, strain selection offers a clear opportunity. The evidence on strain differences shows that some strains can tolerate and utilize elevated CO2 more effectively than others, and that different strains can show different physiological acclimation strategies under high CO2 [N1-R4][N3-R1][N3-R3]. This means that selecting strains adapted to high CO2, NOx, or SOx conditions can improve utilization and removal rates [N1-R1][N1-F1]. Second, process design offers another major opportunity. The evidence on reactor design and simulation shows that reactor geometry, gas flow rate, and gas-phase effects strongly influence performance [N5-R4][N6-R4][N6-R5]. This implies that optimizing bioreactor design, gas distribution, and mass transfer can improve both biomass yield and pollutant capture. Third, operational tuning can improve performance. The evidence indicates that intermittent flue gas aeration can improve CO2 removal efficiency [N2-R1], and that reactor conditions such as gas composition and flow rate affect removal efficiency [N6-R5]. These findings support the idea that process parameters should be tuned rather than fixed.

Trade-offs between biomass production and pollutant removal are important. The evidence suggests that the same reactor can be optimized for biomass, CO2 capture, or pollutant removal, but these objectives may not always be perfectly aligned. For example, the review states that NOx can be used as a nitrogen source when dissolved and oxidized, which may help growth [N1-F1]. This implies that pollutant assimilation can support biomass production. However, the evidence also notes that impurities in flue gas can inhibit growth, so excessive toxicity may reduce biomass yields [N1-F1]. The upstream aggregate on strain performance further reports that growth is limited by gas toxicity, pH, and nutrient availability [N7]. Therefore, the trade-off is real: higher pollutant removal may require more stringent gas-phase control, which can reduce biomass productivity, while maximizing biomass may require less aggressive removal conditions [N1-F1][N7].

Reactor design and simulation conditions strongly influence scalability. The operational search evidence emphasizes that bioreactor design, mechanical design, scale, gas distributor geometry, and impeller geometry are important for performance [N5-R4]. It also notes that the performance of a photobioreactor depends on the equipment and scale [N5-R4]. The simulation evidence further shows that reported strain performance depends on gas composition and simulation conditions [N6-R5][N6-R4]. These findings mean that scalability is not automatic; it depends on whether the reactor can handle high gas flow, maintain stable pH, manage temperature, and support sufficient mass transfer without excessive energy or capital cost. The evidence also suggests that simulation conditions can affect reported performance, so real-world scalability must be validated with actual industrial conditions rather than relying solely on simulated results [N6-R5].

Overall, the system-level constraints are clear: gas flow rate, temperature, and pH must be carefully controlled to avoid toxicity and instability [N6-R5][N5-R2][N1-F1]. Optimization opportunities are strong: strain selection, reactor design, and process tuning can all improve pollutant capture and biomass yield [N1-R1][N3-R1][N5-R4][N6-R5]. Trade-offs between biomass and pollutant removal exist because higher removal may require tighter control, while biomass production may be limited by the same impurities that enable removal [N1-F1][N7]. Reactor design and simulation conditions are critical for scalability, as they shape both performance and the ability to scale up from lab to industrial application [N5-R4][N6-R5].

## Overall conclusion

The evidence supports a nuanced conclusion: different strains of *Chlorella vulgaris* do perform differently when cultivated using coke oven exhaust gases, but the differences are best understood as strain-dependent responses to toxicity, pH, nutrient availability, and reactor conditions, rather than as a single universally superior strain. Some strains show better biomass yield and higher CO2 utilization under flue-gas-like conditions, while others may be more tolerant or efficient at assimilating NOx and SOx. Overall, growth and pollutant capture are not decoupled objectives: maximizing biomass can help pollutant removal, but pollutant removal can also impose limits on biomass production [N1-F1][N7][N8].

## 1) Strain performance: which strains show the highest biomass yield?

The evidence is strongest for the fact that strain performance varies, but it does not provide a complete ranking of all isolates. One direct result is that a *Chlorella sp.* strain designated MTF-15 showed higher growth rates under flue gas from coke oven, hot stove, and similar combustion sources [N1-R1]. This is an important example of strain-specific performance under gas stress. It also suggests that biomass yield is not uniform across strains and that some strains can outperform others in flue-gas cultivation [N1-R1].

At the same time, the evidence does not identify a single “best” strain for coke oven exhaust. Instead, it shows that growth is shaped by both intrinsic strain traits and environmental stress. For example, under produced water stress, *Chlorella vulgaris* showed higher growth and increased antioxidant activity, but the outcome still depended on PW concentration and the specific stress conditions [N3-F3]. This implies that the best biomass yield is context-dependent and likely depends on the specific gas composition and reactor setup rather than a single strain.

## 2) Strain differences affecting CO2 and other gas utilization rates

Strain differences clearly affect utilization rates, especially for CO2. The evidence states that *Chlorella vulgaris* can tolerate and effectively utilize elevated CO2 concentrations, with reported effectiveness under fed-batch culture [N1-R4]. A review also notes that microalgae can assimilate CO2 from flue gas via photosynthesis, and that NOx can be used as a nitrogen source when dissolved and oxidized [N1-F1]. This means that CO2 utilization is largely biological assimilation, while NOx may be partially assimilated or at least partially usable [N1-F1][N1-R4].

For other gases, the evidence is less specific on strain-by-strain utilization rates. The review states that SOx can contribute to low pH and that pH stability helps alleviate inhibition [N1-F1]. It also states that the effect of SOx and NOx on CO2 fixation depends on algae cell density, SOx and NOx concentration, gas flow rate, and reactor design [N6-R5]. This suggests that strain differences affect utilization rates not by a single universal mechanism, but by how well the strain can regulate pH, assimilate nutrients, and tolerate impurities under different gas compositions [N1-F1][N6-R5].

## 3) Are growth limits mainly gas toxicity, pH, or nutrient availability?

Yes: the evidence points to all three as important constraints, with gas toxicity and pH being particularly prominent. The review explicitly states that impurities in flue gas may inhibit microalgal growth [N1-F1]. It also states that SOx can contribute to low pH and that pH stability helps alleviate inhibition [N1-F1]. These findings indicate that pH is a major operational constraint because it directly affects growth and assimilation capacity.

Nutrient availability is also important, but the evidence frames it as part of the broader stress response rather than a primary limiting factor. The produced-water study shows that growth can increase and antioxidant activity stabilize under stress, but the outcome still depends on environmental conditions [N3-F3]. Taken together, the evidence suggests that growth under coke oven exhaust conditions is limited by gas toxicity, pH, and nutrient availability, with pH and toxicity being the most directly reported constraints [N1-F1][N3-F3].

## 4) How do simulation conditions and gas composition affect reported strain performance?

Simulation conditions and gas composition have a major effect on reported performance. The review states that the effect of SOx and NOx on CO2 fixation depends on algae cell density, SOx and NOx concentration, gas flow rate, and reactor design [N6-R5]. Another study on simulated flue gas exposure found that microalgal protein content decreased under simulated power plant emissions, showing that simulation conditions can alter physiological outcomes [N6-R2]. The evidence also emphasizes that CO2 removal and other gas-phase effects depend on reactor parameters and gas composition [N6-R4]. This means that strain performance is highly context-dependent: a strain that performs well in one setup may not do so under another [N6-R5][N6-R4].

The operational evidence reinforces this point. It notes that bioreactor design, mechanical design, scale, gas distributor geometry, and impeller geometry are important for performance [N5-R4]. It also states that the performance of a photobioreactor depends on the equipment and scale [N5-R4]. Together, these findings show that reported strain performance is not just a function of the strain itself, but also of how the system is simulated and operated [N5-R4][N6-R5].

## 5) Pollutant removal capacity and likely pathways

The evidence indicates that *Chlorella vulgaris* can remove multiple pollutants from coke oven exhaust gases, but the reported capacities and pathways differ by pollutant.

### SO2 removal
The evidence supports a mixed mechanism for SO2 removal. The review states that microalgae can remove SOx from flue gas via photosynthesis and that the effect of SOx and NOx on CO2 fixation depends on reactor conditions and gas composition [N6-R5]. It also notes that impurities in flue gas may inhibit microalgal growth [N1-F1]. The evidence further states that SOx can contribute to low pH and that pH stability helps alleviate inhibition [N1-F1]. This suggests that SO2 removal is likely dominated by chemical interaction with the culture medium, with pH regulation playing a major role, and possibly partial biological assimilation under favorable conditions [N1-F1][N6-R5].

### NOx removal
The evidence is stronger for biological assimilation in NOx removal. A review explicitly states that NOx can be utilized as a nitrogen source when dissolved and oxidized in the culture medium [N1-F1]. This supports the idea that NOx removal is primarily biological assimilation, rather than physical adsorption. The evidence also shows that assimilation can support growth, which is relevant to pollutant capture [N1-F1].

### CO removal
The evidence is more indirect for CO. The review notes that microalgae can remove CO2 from flue gas via photosynthesis, and the flue-gas-related evidence emphasizes CO2 mitigation and removal [N1-F1][N6-R5]. However, the provided material does not specifically report CO removal by *Chlorella vulgaris* under coke-oven exhaust conditions. Therefore, while the evidence supports CO2 removal as a major target pollutant, it does not provide a strong direct measure of CO removal under the specified conditions [N1-F1][N6-R5].

### Particulates
The evidence is very limited on particulate capture. The review mentions heavy-metal removal from flue gas as an attractive extension of microalgae use, but it does not specifically discuss particulate capture by *Chlorella vulgaris* [N1-F1]. So, the evidence does not support a confident conclusion about particulate removal capacity.

## 6) Removal pathways: physical adsorption, chemical reaction, or biological assimilation?

The evidence supports a mix of pathways, with biological assimilation being the dominant mechanism for NOx and CO2 removal. For NOx, the review states that it can be utilized as a nitrogen source when dissolved and oxidized [N1-F1], which is clearly biological assimilation. For CO2, the evidence states that microalgae can remove CO2 from flue gas via photosynthesis, which is also biological assimilation [N1-F1][N6-R5]. For SO2, the evidence points more toward chemical interaction and pH regulation, with possible partial assimilation under favorable conditions [N1-F1][N6-R5]. The evidence does not support a dominant role for physical adsorption across the pollutants studied [N1-F1].

## 7) Trade-offs between biomass production and pollutant removal

There is a clear trade-off. The evidence suggests that the same reactor can be optimized for biomass, CO2 capture, or pollutant removal, but these objectives are not perfectly aligned. NOx can be used as a nitrogen source, which may support biomass production [N1-F1]. However, impurities in flue gas can also inhibit growth, so excessive toxicity may reduce biomass yields [N1-F1]. The upstream aggregate on strain performance also reports that growth is limited by gas toxicity, pH, and nutrient availability [N7]. This means that maximizing pollutant removal may require tighter gas-phase control, which can reduce biomass productivity, while maximizing biomass may require less aggressive removal conditions [N1-F1][N7].

## 8) Industrial application: operational constraints and optimization opportunities

Industrial application is feasible, but it requires careful management of operational constraints.

### Operational limits
- **Gas flow rate**: Must be carefully controlled, because the effect of SOx and NOx on CO2 fixation depends on gas flow rate and reactor design [N6-R5].
- **Temperature**: Must be kept within a range that supports growth without thermal stress; the evidence shows that temperature and other operational parameters significantly influence biomass productivity [N5-R2].
- **pH**: Must be stabilized, because impurities can cause low pH and inhibit growth, while stable pH helps alleviate inhibition [N1-F1].
- **Nutrient availability**: Is an underlying constraint, because growth under stress depends on both intrinsic adaptation and extrinsic nutrient conditions [N3-F3].

### Optimization opportunities
- **Strain selection**: Strain differences matter. Some strains can tolerate and utilize elevated CO2 more effectively, and different strains can show different physiological acclimation strategies under high CO2 [N1-R4][N3-R1][N3-R3]. Selecting strains adapted to high CO2, NOx, or SOx conditions can improve utilization and removal rates [N1-R1][N1-F1].
- **Reactor design**: Bioreactor geometry, gas distributor design, scale, and impeller geometry are important for performance [N5-R4]. Optimizing these can improve both biomass yield and pollutant capture.
- **Process tuning**: Intermittent flue gas aeration can improve CO2 removal efficiency, and reactor conditions such as gas composition and flow rate affect removal efficiency [N2-R1][N6-R5].

### Scalability
Reactor design and simulation conditions strongly influence scalability. The evidence shows that the performance of a photobioreactor depends on equipment, scale, and geometry [N5-R4]. It also states that reported strain performance depends on gas composition and simulation conditions [N6-R5]. Therefore, scalability is not automatic; it depends on whether the reactor can handle high gas flow, maintain stable pH, manage temperature, and support sufficient mass transfer without excessive energy or capital cost [N5-R4][N6-R5].

## 9) Final synthesis

In summary, different strains of *Chlorella vulgaris* do perform differently when cultivated using coke oven exhaust gases. Some strains, such as the *Chlorella sp.* strain MTF-15, show higher growth rates under flue gas from coke oven, hot stove, and similar combustion sources [N1-R1]. CO2 utilization is generally strong, especially for strains adapted to high CO2 [N1-R4]. NOx appears to be assimilated as a nitrogen source, while SO2 removal is likely dominated by chemical interaction and pH regulation, with partial biological assimilation under favorable conditions [N1-F1][N6-R5]. Particulate removal is not well supported by the evidence [N1-F1].

The most important constraints are gas toxicity, pH, and nutrient availability, with pH and toxicity being the most directly reported limitations [N1-F1][N3-F3]. Simulation conditions and gas composition strongly affect reported performance, so strain performance is highly context-dependent [N6-R5][N6-R4]. Industrial application is feasible, but it requires careful control of gas flow rate, temperature, and pH, as well as strain selection, reactor design, and process tuning [N5-R2][N5-R4][N6-R5].

The trade-off between biomass production and pollutant removal is real: higher removal may require more stringent gas-phase control, which can reduce biomass productivity, while maximizing biomass may require less aggressive removal conditions [N1-F1][N7]. Overall, the best approach is not a single strain or a single reactor setup, but a combination of strain choice, process design, and operational tuning to balance growth, CO2 capture, and pollutant removal under coke oven exhaust conditions [N1-R1][N1-R4][N6-R5].

Strain performance comparison across growth, biomass, and gas utilization

The evidence available for strain performance under gas conditions similar to coke oven exhaust is mixed but sufficient to identify broad trends rather than a complete strain-by-strain ranking. The clearest direct result is that some microalgae strains, including one Chlorella sp. strain designated MTF-15, showed higher growth rates in flue gas from varied sources of coke oven, hot stove, and similar combustion processes [N1-R1]. This suggests that strain-specific growth response is meaningful under such conditions, though the evidence does not give a full list of competing strains or a standardized comparison across many isolates.

For biomass yield, the evidence points to higher growth in some conditions rather than a single universal “best” strain. In one study, the 100% produced water (PW) treatment gave the highest cell density and growth rate for Chlorella vulgaris, while the 25% PW treatment also showed strong growth behavior [N3-F3]. This is relevant because it shows that strain adaptation and environmental stress can strongly influence biomass outcomes, even though the condition here is PW rather than coke oven exhaust. It also implies that biomass yield is not fixed by strain alone: growth can be shaped by both intrinsic strain traits and extrinsic environmental stressors.

CO2 utilization and gas utilization rates are more clearly supported in the evidence. Chlorella vulgaris can tolerate and effectively utilize elevated CO2 concentrations, with reported effectiveness under fed-batch culture [N1-R4]. A review also states that microalgae can assimilate CO2 from flue gas via photosynthesis and that NOx can be used as a nitrogen source when dissolved and oxidized, which may help growth [N1-F1]. This is important because it indicates that CO2 utilization is often biological assimilation, rather than merely a physical absorption effect. The evidence also notes that the impurities in flue gas may inhibit microalgal growth, so gas toxicity is a real constraint [N1-F1].

For other gases, the evidence is less specific on exact utilization rates for NOx and SO2. A review states that SOx may contribute to low pH and that pH stability can alleviate inhibition effects [N1-F1]. It also states that NOx can be utilized as a nitrogen source when dissolved and oxidized [N1-F1]. These statements suggest that gas utilization is not uniform: NOx appears to be assimilated or at least partially usable, whereas SOx may primarily affect pH and inhibit growth rather than being directly assimilated. The evidence does not clearly separate strain-specific utilization rates for these gases, so any comparison across strains is weakly supported by the provided material.

Growth limitation factors are better documented. The evidence explicitly states that impurities in flue gas may inhibit microalgal growth [N1-F1]. It also notes that SOx can contribute to low pH and that pH stability helps alleviate inhibition [N1-F1]. Additionally, the evidence on produced water shows that strain adaptation is possible but that growth is still influenced by stress and nutrient conditions [N3-F3]. Taken together, this suggests that growth under coke oven exhaust conditions is limited by gas toxicity and pH, with nutrient availability also playing a role when the culture is stressed.

Simulation conditions and gas composition strongly affect reported performance. The review notes that the effect of SOx and NOx on CO2 fixation depends on algae cell density, SOx and NOx concentration, gas flow rate, and reactor design [N6-R5]. Another study on simulated flue gas exposure found that microalgal protein content decreased under simulated power plant emissions, showing that simulated conditions can alter physiological outcomes [N6-R2]. The evidence also emphasizes that CO2 removal and other gas-phase effects depend on reactor parameters and gas composition [N6-R4]. These findings indicate that reported strain performance is highly context-dependent: a strain that performs well in one gas composition or reactor setup may not do so under another.

Overall, the evidence supports a cautious conclusion: some strains of Chlorella vulgaris, particularly those adapted to high CO2 or flue-gas-like conditions, can outperform others in biomass yield and CO2 utilization under coke oven exhaust conditions [N1-R1][N1-R4][N1-F1]. However, the evidence does not provide a strong enough comparative ranking of strains to identify a single “best” strain, and performance is heavily influenced by gas toxicity, pH, nutrient availability, and simulation conditions [N1-F1][N6-R5]. The evidence indicates that Chlorella vulgaris can remove multiple pollutants from flue gas, but the reported capacities and mechanisms differ by pollutant. For SO2, the evidence is consistent with removal through a combination of chemical and biological pathways. A review states that microalgae can remove SOx from flue gas via photosynthesis and that the effect of SOx and NOx on CO2 fixation depends on reactor conditions and gas composition [N6-R5]. Another review notes that the impurities in flue gas may inhibit microalgal growth, implying that removal is not simply physical adsorption but is constrained by toxicity and environmental stress [N1-F1]. The evidence also suggests that SOx can lower pH and that pH stability helps alleviate inhibition, which points to a chemical reaction pathway in addition to biological assimilation [N1-F1]. Overall, the evidence supports a mixed mechanism for SO2 removal: chemical interaction with the culture medium and possible biological assimilation, with removal efficiency depending on gas composition and reactor design [N1-F1][N6-R5].

For NOx, the evidence is more directly supportive of biological assimilation. A review explicitly states that NOx can be utilized as a nitrogen source when dissolved and oxidized in the culture medium [N1-F1]. A separate study on microalgal-bacterial systems reports a maximum CO2 removal efficiency of 55.3% at 0.15% CO2 in a membrane photobioreactor and mentions Chlorella vulgaris as part of the system [N2-R2]. While this does not directly measure NOx removal, it supports the idea that NOx can be assimilated into the culture when available in oxidized form. The evidence also indicates that NOx removal is part of a broader pollutant-removal process that may involve assimilation rather than purely physical adsorption [N1-F1].

For CO, the evidence is more indirect. The review notes that microalgae can remove CO2 from flue gas via photosynthesis, and the flue-gas-related evidence emphasizes CO2 mitigation and removal [N1-F1][N6-R5]. However, the provided material does not specifically report CO removal by Chlorella vulgaris under coke oven exhaust conditions. The closest related statement is that microalgae removal of CO2 depends on reactor conditions and gas composition [N6-R5]. Therefore, while the evidence supports CO2 removal as a major target pollutant, it does not provide a strong direct measure of CO removal for Chlorella vulgaris under coke-oven exhaust conditions.

For particulates, the evidence is very limited. The review mentions heavy-metal removal from flue gas as an attractive extension of microalgae use, but it does not specifically discuss particulate capture by Chlorella vulgaris [N1-F1]. The provided material therefore does not support a confident conclusion about particulate removal capacity.

The likely removal pathways are therefore: SO2 is removed by chemical interaction and possible assimilation, NOx by biological assimilation as nitrogen, CO2 by biological assimilation via photosynthesis, and particulates are not well supported by the evidence provided. The evidence also makes clear that removal is not dominated by physical adsorption in the way that some gas-phase processes might be; instead, it is constrained by toxicity, pH, and nutrient availability [N1-F1][N6-R5]. The removal efficiency of each pollutant depends strongly on gas composition and simulation conditions, including SOx and NOx concentration, cell density, gas flow rate, and reactor design [N6-R5].

Physiological and metabolic responses are relevant to explaining these differences. The evidence on Chlorella vulgaris exposed to produced water shows that growth can increase and antioxidant activity stabilize under stress, indicating that physiological adaptation is important for survival and pollutant removal [N3-F3]. A separate study on Chlorella strains exposed to high CO2 found different metabolic acclimation strategies and intracellular pH regulation, showing that strain-specific physiology can shape tolerance and utilization under gas stress [N3-R1][N3-R3]. These findings support the idea that pollutant removal capacity varies by strain because some strains may better regulate pH, stress responses, and nutrient assimilation than others [N3-F3][N3-R1].

In summary, the evidence suggests that Chlorella vulgaris can effectively remove SO2 and NOx from coke oven exhaust gases, with NOx more clearly assimilated as a nitrogen source and SO2 removed partly through chemical and partly through biological mechanisms [N1-F1][N6-R5]. CO2 removal is also strong, but the evidence does not provide a direct measure of CO removal under coke-oven conditions [N1-F1][N6-R5]. Pollutant removal is likely dominated by biological assimilation for NOx and CO2, with chemical interaction and pH regulation playing important roles for SO2 [N1-F1][N6-R5]. Gas composition and simulation conditions strongly affect removal efficiency, making strain performance highly context-dependent [N6-R5].

First, gas flow rate is an important constraint because the review states that the effect of SOx and NOx on CO2 fixation depends on SOx and NOx concentration, gas flow rate, and reactor design [N6-R5]. The operational search evidence also suggests that reactor design and gas-phase effects are central to performance, with simulation conditions and gas composition strongly affecting reported strain performance [N5-R4][N6-R4]. This implies that gas flow rate cannot be arbitrarily increased without risking toxicity, mass transfer limitations, or reduced biomass productivity.

Second, temperature is an operational limit because the evidence on industrial exhaust gas cultivation notes that temperature affects microalgal growth and bioreactor performance [N5-R1][N5-R2]. The operational search evidence further shows that temperature and other operational parameters can significantly influence biomass productivity, with the example of C. vulgaris showing high biomass productivities up to 30°C with moderate to high CO2 [N5-R2]. This indicates that temperature is not universally optimal across all conditions; rather, it must be kept within a range that balances growth and pollutant capture while avoiding thermal stress or denaturation of enzymes and other physiological processes.

Third, pH is a major constraint because the review explicitly states that impurities in flue gas may inhibit microalgal growth and that SOx can contribute to low pH, which can be alleviated by maintaining a stable pH level [N1-F1]. The evidence on produced water also shows that growth can increase and antioxidant activity stabilize under stress, but the outcome still depends on environmental conditions [N3-F3]. Taken together, these findings suggest that pH control is essential: unstable or low pH can limit biomass production and pollutant removal, while stable pH supports better tolerance and assimilation of nutrients and pollutants [N1-F1][N3-F3].

Operational limits for stable cultivation therefore include: gas flow rate must be carefully controlled to avoid toxicity and mass transfer bottlenecks [N6-R5]; temperature should remain within a range that supports growth without thermal stress [N5-R2]; and pH should be stabilized to prevent inhibition from SOx and other impurities [N1-F1]. The evidence also suggests that nutrient availability is an underlying constraint, because growth under stress is shaped by both intrinsic strain adaptation and extrinsic nutrient conditions [N3-F3].

Opportunities to improve pollutant capture are substantial and are supported by both strain and system evidence. First, strain selection offers a clear opportunity. The evidence on strain differences shows that some strains can tolerate and utilize elevated CO2 more effectively than others, and that different strains can show different physiological acclimation strategies under high CO2 [N1-R4][N3-R1][N3-R3]. This means that selecting strains adapted to high CO2, NOx, or SOx conditions can improve utilization and removal rates [N1-R1][N1-F1]. Second, process design offers another major opportunity. The evidence on reactor design and simulation shows that reactor geometry, gas flow rate, and gas-phase effects strongly influence performance [N5-R4][N6-R4][N6-R5]. These findings support the idea that process parameters should be tuned rather than fixed.

For example, the review states that NOx can be used as a nitrogen source when dissolved and oxidized, which may help growth [N1-F1]. This implies that pollutant assimilation can support biomass production. However, the evidence also notes that impurities in flue gas can inhibit growth, so excessive toxicity may reduce biomass yields [N1-F1]. Therefore, the trade-off is real: higher pollutant removal may require more stringent gas-phase control, which can reduce biomass productivity, while maximizing biomass may require less aggressive removal conditions [N1-F1][N7].

Reactor design and simulation conditions strongly influence scalability. The operational search evidence emphasizes that bioreactor design, mechanical design, scale, gas distributor geometry, and impeller geometry are important for performance [N5-R4]. ## Overall conclusion

The evidence supports a nuanced conclusion: different strains of *Chlorella vulgaris* do perform differently when cultivated using coke oven exhaust gases, but the differences are best understood as strain-dependent responses to toxicity, pH, nutrient availability, and reactor conditions, rather than as a single universally superior strain. Some strains show better biomass yield and higher CO2 utilization under flue-gas-like conditions, while others may be more tolerant or efficient at assimilating NOx and SOx. Overall, growth and pollutant capture are not decoupled objectives: maximizing biomass can help pollutant removal, but pollutant removal can also impose limits on biomass production [N1-F1][N7][N8].

## 1) Strain performance: which strains show the highest biomass yield?

The evidence is strongest for the fact that strain performance varies, but it does not provide a complete ranking of all isolates. One direct result is that a *Chlorella sp.* strain designated MTF-15 showed higher growth rates under flue gas from coke oven, hot stove, and similar combustion sources [N1-R1]. This is an important example of strain-specific performance under gas stress. It also suggests that biomass yield is not uniform across strains and that some strains can outperform others in flue-gas cultivation [N1-R1].

At the same time, the evidence does not identify a single “best” strain for coke oven exhaust. Instead, it shows that growth is shaped by both intrinsic strain traits and environmental stress. For example, under produced water stress, *Chlorella vulgaris* showed higher growth and increased antioxidant activity, but the outcome still depended on PW concentration and the specific stress conditions [N3-F3]. This implies that the best biomass yield is context-dependent and likely depends on the specific gas composition and reactor setup rather than a single strain.

## 2) Strain differences affecting CO2 and other gas utilization rates

Strain differences clearly affect utilization rates, especially for CO2. The evidence states that *Chlorella vulgaris* can tolerate and effectively utilize elevated CO2 concentrations, with reported effectiveness under fed-batch culture [N1-R4]. A review also notes that microalgae can assimilate CO2 from flue gas via photosynthesis, and that NOx can be used as a nitrogen source when dissolved and oxidized [N1-F1]. This means that CO2 utilization is largely biological assimilation, while NOx may be partially assimilated or at least partially usable [N1-F1][N1-R4].

For other gases, the evidence is less specific on strain-by-strain utilization rates. The review states that SOx can contribute to low pH and that pH stability helps alleviate inhibition [N1-F1]. It also states that the effect of SOx and NOx on CO2 fixation depends on algae cell density, SOx and NOx concentration, gas flow rate, and reactor design [N6-R5]. This suggests that strain differences affect utilization rates not by a single universal mechanism, but by how well the strain can regulate pH, assimilate nutrients, and tolerate impurities under different gas compositions [N1-F1][N6-R5].

## 3) Are growth limits mainly gas toxicity, pH, or nutrient availability?

Yes: the evidence points to all three as important constraints, with gas toxicity and pH being particularly prominent. The review explicitly states that impurities in flue gas may inhibit microalgal growth [N1-F1]. It also states that SOx can contribute to low pH and that pH stability helps alleviate inhibition [N1-F1]. These findings indicate that pH is a major operational constraint because it directly affects growth and assimilation capacity.

Nutrient availability is also important, but the evidence frames it as part of the broader stress response rather than a primary limiting factor. The produced-water study shows that growth can increase and antioxidant activity stabilize under stress, but the outcome still depends on environmental conditions [N3-F3]. Taken together, the evidence suggests that growth under coke oven exhaust conditions is limited by gas toxicity, pH, and nutrient availability, with pH and toxicity being the most directly reported constraints [N1-F1][N3-F3].

## 4) How do simulation conditions and gas composition affect reported strain performance?

Simulation conditions and gas composition have a major effect on reported performance. The review states that the effect of SOx and NOx on CO2 fixation depends on algae cell density, SOx and NOx concentration, gas flow rate, and reactor design [N6-R5]. Another study on simulated flue gas exposure found that microalgal protein content decreased under simulated power plant emissions, showing that simulation conditions can alter physiological outcomes [N6-R2]. The evidence also emphasizes that CO2 removal and other gas-phase effects depend on reactor parameters and gas composition [N6-R4]. This means that strain performance is highly context-dependent: a strain that performs well in one setup may not do so under another [N6-R5][N6-R4].

The operational evidence reinforces this point. It notes that bioreactor design, mechanical design, scale, gas distributor geometry, and impeller geometry are important for performance [N5-R4]. It also states that the performance of a photobioreactor depends on the equipment and scale [N5-R4]. Together, these findings show that reported strain performance is not just a function of the strain itself, but also of how the system is simulated and operated [N5-R4][N6-R5].

## 5) Pollutant removal capacity and likely pathways

The evidence indicates that *Chlorella vulgaris* can remove multiple pollutants from coke oven exhaust gases, but the reported capacities and pathways differ by pollutant.

### SO2 removal
The evidence supports a mixed mechanism for SO2 removal. The review states that microalgae can remove SOx from flue gas via photosynthesis and that the effect of SOx and NOx on CO2 fixation depends on reactor conditions and gas composition [N6-R5]. It also notes that impurities in flue gas may inhibit microalgal growth [N1-F1]. The evidence further states that SOx can contribute to low pH and that pH stability helps alleviate inhibition [N1-F1]. This suggests that SO2 removal is likely dominated by chemical interaction with the culture medium, with pH regulation playing a major role, and possibly partial biological assimilation under favorable conditions [N1-F1][N6-R5].

### NOx removal
The evidence is stronger for biological assimilation in NOx removal. A review explicitly states that NOx can be utilized as a nitrogen source when dissolved and oxidized in the culture medium [N1-F1]. This supports the idea that NOx removal is primarily biological assimilation, rather than physical adsorption. The evidence also shows that assimilation can support growth, which is relevant to pollutant capture [N1-F1].

### CO removal
The evidence is more indirect for CO. The review notes that microalgae can remove CO2 from flue gas via photosynthesis, and the flue-gas-related evidence emphasizes CO2 mitigation and removal [N1-F1][N6-R5]. However, the provided material does not specifically report CO removal by *Chlorella vulgaris* under coke-oven exhaust conditions. Therefore, while the evidence supports CO2 removal as a major target pollutant, it does not provide a strong direct measure of CO removal under the specified conditions [N1-F1][N6-R5].

### Particulates
The evidence is very limited on particulate capture. The review mentions heavy-metal removal from flue gas as an attractive extension of microalgae use, but it does not specifically discuss particulate capture by *Chlorella vulgaris* [N1-F1]. So, the evidence does not support a confident conclusion about particulate removal capacity.

## 6) Removal pathways: physical adsorption, chemical reaction, or biological assimilation?

The evidence supports a mix of pathways, with biological assimilation being the dominant mechanism for NOx and CO2 removal. For NOx, the review states that it can be utilized as a nitrogen source when dissolved and oxidized [N1-F1], which is clearly biological assimilation. For CO2, the evidence states that microalgae can remove CO2 from flue gas via photosynthesis, which is also biological assimilation [N1-F1][N6-R5]. For SO2, the evidence points more toward chemical interaction and pH regulation, with possible partial assimilation under favorable conditions [N1-F1][N6-R5]. The evidence does not support a dominant role for physical adsorption across the pollutants studied [N1-F1].

## 7) Trade-offs between biomass production and pollutant removal

There is a clear trade-off. The evidence suggests that the same reactor can be optimized for biomass, CO2 capture, or pollutant removal, but these objectives are not perfectly aligned. NOx can be used as a nitrogen source, which may support biomass production [N1-F1]. However, impurities in flue gas can also inhibit growth, so excessive toxicity may reduce biomass yields [N1-F1]. The upstream aggregate on strain performance also reports that growth is limited by gas toxicity, pH, and nutrient availability [N7]. This means that maximizing pollutant removal may require tighter gas-phase control, which can reduce biomass productivity, while maximizing biomass may require less aggressive removal conditions [N1-F1][N7].

## 8) Industrial application: operational constraints and optimization opportunities

Industrial application is feasible, but it requires careful management of operational constraints.

### Operational limits
- **Gas flow rate**: Must be carefully controlled, because the effect of SOx and NOx on CO2 fixation depends on gas flow rate and reactor design [N6-R5].
- **Temperature**: Must be kept within a range that supports growth without thermal stress; the evidence shows that temperature and other operational parameters significantly influence biomass productivity [N5-R2].
- **pH**: Must be stabilized, because impurities can cause low pH and inhibit growth, while stable pH helps alleviate inhibition [N1-F1].
- **Nutrient availability**: Is an underlying constraint, because growth under stress depends on both intrinsic adaptation and extrinsic nutrient conditions [N3-F3].

### Optimization opportunities
- **Strain selection**: Strain differences matter. Some strains can tolerate and utilize elevated CO2 more effectively, and different strains can show different physiological acclimation strategies under high CO2 [N1-R4][N3-R1][N3-R3]. Selecting strains adapted to high CO2, NOx, or SOx conditions can improve utilization and removal rates [N1-R1][N1-F1].
- **Reactor design**: Bioreactor geometry, gas distributor design, scale, and impeller geometry are important for performance [N5-R4]. Optimizing these can improve both biomass yield and pollutant capture.
- **Process tuning**: Intermittent flue gas aeration can improve CO2 removal efficiency, and reactor conditions such as gas composition and flow rate affect removal efficiency [N2-R1][N6-R5].

### Scalability
Reactor design and simulation conditions strongly influence scalability. The evidence shows that the performance of a photobioreactor depends on equipment, scale, and geometry [N5-R4]. It also states that reported strain performance depends on gas composition and simulation conditions [N6-R5]. Therefore, scalability is not automatic; it depends on whether the reactor can handle high gas flow, maintain stable pH, manage temperature, and support sufficient mass transfer without excessive energy or capital cost [N5-R4][N6-R5].

## 9) Final synthesis

In summary, different strains of *Chlorella vulgaris* do perform differently when cultivated using coke oven exhaust gases. Some strains, such as the *Chlorella sp.* strain MTF-15, show higher growth rates under flue gas from coke oven, hot stove, and similar combustion sources [N1-R1]. CO2 utilization is generally strong, especially for strains adapted to high CO2 [N1-R4]. NOx appears to be assimilated as a nitrogen source, while SO2 removal is likely dominated by chemical interaction and pH regulation, with partial biological assimilation under favorable conditions [N1-F1][N6-R5]. Particulate removal is not well supported by the evidence [N1-F1].

The most important constraints are gas toxicity, pH, and nutrient availability, with pH and toxicity being the most directly reported limitations [N1-F1][N3-F3]. Simulation conditions and gas composition strongly affect reported performance, so strain performance is highly context-dependent [N6-R5][N6-R4]. Industrial application is feasible, but it requires careful control of gas flow rate, temperature, and pH, as well as strain selection, reactor design, and process tuning [N5-R2][N5-R4][N6-R5].

The trade-off between biomass production and pollutant removal is real: higher removal may require more stringent gas-phase control, which can reduce biomass productivity, while maximizing biomass may require less aggressive removal conditions [N1-F1][N7]. Overall, the best approach is not a single strain or a single reactor setup, but a combination of strain choice, process design, and operational tuning to balance growth, CO2 capture, and pollutant removal under coke oven exhaust conditions [N1-R1][N1-R4][N6-R5].
